name: Umberleigh House and Holy Trinity Chapel
text: Your train passes near Umberleigh House, on the train's {side}, a Georgian farmhouse listed Grade I with the ruins of the medieval chapel of the Holy Trinity beside it. The Devon historian Tristram Risdon wrote that the site was once a palace of the Saxon king Æthelstan.

name: Barnstaple Long Bridge
text: Your train passes near Barnstaple's Long Bridge over the River Taw, on the train's {side}, one of the largest medieval bridges in Britain. A will of 1274 left money for its upkeep.

name: Rougemont Castle
text: Your train passes near Rougemont Castle, on the train's {side}, built into a corner of Exeter's Roman walls from 1068, after the city rebelled against William the Conqueror. In 1682 the three Devon Witches, the last people in England executed for witchcraft, were tried there.

name: Taunton Castle
text: Your train passes near Taunton Castle, on the train's {side}, now the Museum of Somerset. In its Great Hall in 1685 Judge Jeffreys held the Bloody Assizes after the Monmouth Rebellion, and 144 men were hanged.

name: Haynes Motor Museum
text: Your train passes near the Haynes Motor Museum at Sparkford, on the train's {side}, with more than 300 cars and motorcycles. It was founded in 1985 by John Haynes, of the Haynes workshop manuals, in a disused sawmill.

name: Newton Surmaville
text: Your train passes near Newton Surmaville, on the train's {side}, a house built between 1608 and 1612 for the clothier Robert Harbin and listed Grade I.

name: Upbury Farm, Yetminster
text: Your train passes near Upbury Farm in Yetminster, on the train's {side}, where a blue plaque remembers the farmer Benjamin Jesty, born in the village. In 1774, some 20 years before Edward Jenner's vaccine, he used cowpox to give immunity against smallpox.

name: St Andrew's Church, Yetminster
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church in Yetminster, on the train's {side}, listed Grade I and mostly from the mid-1400s. Its faceless clock, some 300 years old, chimes the national anthem every three hours.

name: Church of St Peter and St Paul, Cattistock
text: Your train passes near the church at Cattistock, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 1800s by Sir George Gilbert Scott and his son. The son's tall tower earned it the name "Cathedral of the Frome Valley".

name: Poundbury Camp
text: Your train runs in a tunnel beneath Poundbury Camp, an Iron Age hillfort above Dorchester. Brunel wanted a cutting through it, but local outrage meant the more expensive tunnel was built instead.

name: Maumbury Rings
text: Your train passes near Maumbury Rings, on the train's {side}, a Neolithic henge that the Romans made into an amphitheatre and the Civil War into an artillery fort. In 1846 the route planned for the Southampton and Dorchester Railway was changed to spare it.

name: Ridgeway Hill Viking burial pit
text: Your train passes near Ridgeway Hill, on the train's {side}, where in June 2009 archaeologists found a pit holding the remains of 54 Scandinavian men, executed some time between 970 and 1025. They are thought to have been Vikings killed by the local Anglo-Saxons.

name: King's Statue, Weymouth
text: Your train passes near the King's Statue in Weymouth, on the train's {side}, put up in 1809 for George III's Golden Jubilee. The king came to Weymouth on holiday 14 times, the first in 1789.

name: Marston Moat
text: Your train passes near Marston Moat, on the train's {side}, the moat of a fortified manor house held by the Bigot family before 1195. There is some evidence they fortified it without the king's licence; that, and an insult to the king's messenger, cost Richard Bigot his lands.

name: Berkley House
text: Your train passes near Berkley House, on the train's {side}, home of Squire Thomas Prowse, who built the church of St Mary beside it in 1751. The church has a glazed cupola over its nave.

name: Handle House, Studley Mills
text: Your train passes near the Handle House at Studley Mills in Trowbridge, on the train's {side}, which straddles the River Biss. It was used to dry and store teasels, which were used to raise the nap of cloth.

name: Bradford-on-Avon Tithe Barn
text: Your train passes near the tithe barn at Barton Farm, on the train's {side}, built in the 1330s for the nuns of Shaftesbury Abbey, the richest nunnery in England. It is listed Grade I and looked after by English Heritage.

name: St Laurence's Church, Bradford-on-Avon
text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church in Bradford-on-Avon, on the train's {side}, one of very few Anglo-Saxon churches in England without later medieval changes. For many years it was used as a school and a cottage, until William Jones, rector of the parish church of Holy Trinity, rediscovered it in 1856.

name: Avoncliff Aqueduct
text: Your train passes under Avoncliff Aqueduct, next to Avoncliff station, which carries the Kennet and Avon Canal over the River Avon and the railway. It was built by John Rennie and John Thomas between 1797 and 1801.

name: Claverton Pumping Station
text: Your train passes near Claverton Pumping Station, on the train's {side}, built by John Rennie between 1809 and 1813. The River Avon turns its great water wheel, which pumps water 48 feet up to the Kennet and Avon Canal, on the other side of the railway.

name: Yelde Hall, Chippenham
text: Your train passes near the Yelde Hall in Chippenham's Market Place, on the train's {side}, built in about 1450 and once the meeting place of Chippenham Borough Council. It is listed Grade I.

name: Staverton Mill
text: Your train passes near Staverton Mill, on the train's {side}, a mill on the River Avon since the Domesday Book. Once a woollen mill and later a Nestlé milk factory, it makes breakfast cereals: Shredded Wheat and Shreddies moved there in 2007.

name: Health Hydro, Swindon
text: Your train passes near the Health Hydro in Swindon, on the train's {side}, built for the Great Western Railway's Medical Fund Society. Its Turkish baths carry on a service begun for railway workers and their families in 1868, the longest-surviving Victorian Turkish baths in the world; in 1948 the fund's medical services became part of the new NHS.

name: Stoke Gifford depot
text: Your train passes near Stoke Gifford depot, on the train's {side}, built on a triangle of land between three railway lines. It was built to look after Great Western Railway's Class 800 trains, which entered service in 2017.

name: New Orphan Houses, Ashley Down
text: Your train passes near the New Orphan Houses on Ashley Down, on the train's {side}, built between 1849 and 1870 by George Müller. Their five houses held 2,050 children at a time, and Müller never asked anyone for money to run them.

name: St Werburgh's Church, Bristol
text: Your train passes near St Werburgh's Church, on the train's {side}, a medieval church that stood in Corn Street in the old city until 1879, when it was taken down and rebuilt here. Its 14th-century tower was moved stone by stone; the church is now a climbing centre.

name: St Paul's Church, Bristol
text: Your train passes near St Paul's Church in Portland Square, on the train's {side}, begun in 1789 and listed Grade I. It closed in 1988 and is now Circomedia, a circus school.

name: Redland Chapel
text: Your train passes near Redland Chapel, on the train's {side}, built in 1742 as a private chapel for John Cossins of Redland Court and listed Grade I. Now the parish church, it is unusual in having no patron saint.

name: Clifton Lido
text: Your train passes near the Lido in Clifton, on the train's {side}, opened as the Clifton Victoria Baths in 1850. It closed in 1990 and was considered for demolition, but was restored and reopened in 2008.

name: Abona Roman town
text: Your train runs through the site of Abona, a small Roman port town at the mouth of the River Trym. Much Roman material was dug up when the dock at Sea Mills was built.

name: Kings Weston House
text: Your train passes near Kings Weston House, on the train's {side}, built between 1712 and 1719 to designs by Sir John Vanbrugh for the lawyer and politician Edward Southwell.

name: Avonmouth Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Avonmouth Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carries the M5 over the River Avon. It is 4,554 feet long, with a main span of 538 feet.

name: Pill Lifeboat Station
text: Your train passes near Pill, across the river on the train's {side}, where the RNLI kept a lifeboat for little more than three years, from July 1971 to November 1974.

name: Avonmouth Docks
text: Your train passes near Avonmouth Docks, on the train's {side}, part of the Port of Bristol where the Avon meets the Severn estuary. Today they are one of the UK's main ports for chilled foods, especially fruit and vegetables.

name: Lawrence Weston Wind Turbine
text: Your train passes near the Lawrence Weston wind turbine, on the train's {side}, owned by the community it helps to fund. When it started turning in May 2023 it was the tallest onshore wind turbine in England, 150 metres to the tip of its blades.

name: Northern Storm Water Interceptor
text: Your train passes near Bristol's Northern Storm Water Interceptor, on the train's {side}: a tunnel about 16 feet across that carries floodwater from the River Frome at Eastville three miles under the city to the Avon Gorge. It was finished in 1962.

name: Brunel's Old Station, Temple Meads
text: Your train passes near Brunel's original Temple Meads station, on the train's {side}, opened on August 31st 1840 as the western end of the Great Western Railway. It is listed Grade I and no longer used by trains.

name: St Mary Redcliffe
text: Your train passes near St Mary Redcliffe, on the train's {side}, whose spire is 274 feet high. Elizabeth I is said to have called it "the fairest, goodliest and most famous parish church in England" on a visit in 1574.

name: St John the Baptist's Church, Bedminster
text: Your train passes near the site of St John the Baptist's Church in Bedminster, on the train's {side}, one of Bristol's oldest churches, first recorded in 1003. It was gutted in the Blitz in November 1940 and in 1967 the council approved the demolition of its ruins.

name: Tyntesfield
text: Your train passes near the park of Tyntesfield, on the train's {side}, around a Victorian Gothic house remodelled in the 1860s for William Gibbs, whose fortune came from guano. The National Trust bought it in 2002.
